threads_text: China's AI stock boom just popped: the STAR50 index of AI and chip leaders fell about 40% in under four months and erased roughly $480 billion, Reuters reports. Wall Street's AI stocks have only slipped about 6% by comparison. Is the US next, or is this a China only problem?
caption:
China's index of AI and chip leaders, the STAR50, fell about 40% in under four months, erasing roughly $480 billion, Reuters reports.
Retail favorites like robot maker Unitree have roughly halved since their debuts.
The US Nasdaq is down only about 6% from its record.

Is the US AI trade next, or is this a China only crash?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

paragraphs.text: China's STAR50 index, which tracks leading artificial intelligence and semiconductor companies on the mainland, fell about 40% in under four months and erased roughly $480 billion in market value, according to a Reuters analysis published on October 26, 2026. Reuters said China's broad blue chip index is down about 20% from its June highs.

The decline ended a two year rally that began with promises of economic stimulus and stalled Beijing's push for a slow bull market of steady gains, Reuters reported. By comparison, the Nasdaq in the United States was about 6% below a record high it set three weeks earlier.

Reuters found no obvious trigger for the selloff. Traders pointed to high prices, tax bills and the risk that the United States or other countries could ban Chinese equipment from data centers. According to Goldman Sachs figures cited by Reuters, AI stocks account for 42% of market capitalization and 57% of turnover across mainland A shares and Hong Kong H shares, which means the slump reaches far beyond a niche corner of the market.

Several of the market's most popular names have been hit hard. Robot maker Unitree, whose listing was about 8,000 times oversubscribed by retail buyers, has roughly halved since it began trading in August. Chipmaker CXMT lost more than a quarter of its value over the past month. Graphics chip designers MetaX Integrated Circuits and Moore Threads, which jumped about 700% and 400% on their market debuts, have each roughly halved since July.

Optical component makers Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink are down about 60% from their June and July highs, in part because Washington is moving toward barring them from supplying US data centers, Reuters reported.

Even after the drop, the STAR50 trades at about 100 times trailing earnings, down from nearly 250 times at its peak. The Nasdaq 100 trades at about 30 times. A Beijing based fund manager, Dong Baozhen, told Reuters the market had turned into a speculative bull run and that he now sees the bubble bursting.

Geo News, citing Bloomberg data, reported that Chinese state backed investors poured 128.7 billion yuan, about $19 billion, into nine exchange traded funds in the latest week, the largest weekly inflow since April 2025. It also reported that the CSI 300 has entered bear market territory after ten straight weekly declines.

Not every investor is retreating. Goldman Sachs included Innolight and CXMT in a revamped list of recommended Chinese AI stocks, and BNP Paribas strategist William Bratton said the market offers opportunities for careful investors, according to Reuters. HSBC research cited in the report found that Asia funds remain overweight China, although they have been net sellers over the past three months. Analysts quoted by Reuters expect the slump to slow fundraising by technology companies and to discourage some planned listings.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the gap between China and the United States matters more than the size of the drop. Chinese AI shares were priced for a future that retail buyers rushed to own, and export risks hit them directly. US AI stocks face some of the same demand questions, but so far the market has treated them very differently.
The next signal to watch is whether state backed buying slows the decline, and whether Chinese AI and chip companies delay planned listings as Reuters sources expect.
